subject: Architecture
title: Vertical Farms: Skyscrapers That Feed Cities
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Vertical Farms: Skyscrapers That Feed Cities.

hook.text: What if skyscrapers grew food instead of housing offices? Vertical farms are making it real.

buildup.text: Indoor farms stack growing trays floor by floor, using LED lights and hydroponics instead of soil and sun.

discovery.text: A single vertical farm tower can grow the equivalent of 700 acres of traditional farmland.

twist.text: Energy costs are huge — LED lighting uses so much electricity that most vertical farms aren't profitable yet.

climax.text: Singapore, with almost no farmland, is investing heavily in vertical farms for food security.

punchline.text: Cities that can't spread out might grow up — literally.

quiz.question: What is the biggest challenge facing vertical farms today?
options: Plants cannot grow without natural sunlight
High energy costs for LED lighting make most unprofitable
Building codes prohibit farming inside skyscrapers

details.summary: Vertical farms grow crops inside tall buildings using hydroponics, LED lighting, and climate control, producing food year-round regardless of weather or season. They use up to 95% less water than field farming and can be located in city centers, reducing transportation emissions and food miles.
details.whyItMatters: Vertical farms could decouple food production from climate and geography. As urban populations grow and arable land shrinks, growing food inside buildings may become essential for feeding cities sustainably.
takeaways: Vertical farms use hydroponics and LEDs to grow food indoors
They use up to 95% less water than conventional farming
Urban location reduces food miles and transportation emissions

faq.question: Can vertical farms actually feed a city?
faq.answer: Not entirely — current technology works best for leafy greens, herbs, and some fruits. Staple crops like wheat and rice remain impractical indoors due to energy costs. Vertical farms supplement urban food supply rather than replacing traditional agriculture entirely.

faq.question: Are vertical farms economically viable?
faq.answer: Increasingly so for high-value crops like lettuce, basil, and strawberries. Energy costs for lighting remain the biggest expense. As LED efficiency improves and renewable energy costs fall, the economics continue to improve, especially in regions with expensive imported produce.
